info.title: Knee MRI model weights: twelve findings
info.subtitle: Trained CoAtNet weights that score twelve findings on a knee MRI study
info.description:
![Dread Development — Johnathan Wagner](https://bojackdidit.github.io/dread-cinematic-banner/dread-orbit-web.webp)

[![Kaggle](https://bojackdidit.github.io/dread-cinematic-banner/buttons/kaggle-bar.png)](https://www.kaggle.com/dreaddevelopment) [![GitHub](https://bojackdidit.github.io/dread-cinematic-banner/buttons/github-bar.png)](https://github.com/Bojackdidit) [![Website](https://bojackdidit.github.io/dread-cinematic-banner/buttons/website-bar.png)](https://dreaddevelopment.com) [![Email](https://bojackdidit.github.io/dread-cinematic-banner/buttons/email-bar.png)](mailto:john@dreaddevelopment.com)

Two trained checkpoints for a model that reads a knee MRI study and scores twelve findings at once: ACL tear, MCL tear, medial and lateral meniscus tears, osteoarthritis in the medial, lateral and patellofemoral compartments, joint effusion, synovitis, a Baker's cyst, bone contusion and fracture.

The model scores 0.924 on the public leaderboard of the RSNA Knee Abnormality Detection competition as a single model, with no ensembling and no test-time augmentation.

WHAT IS IN THE FILES

Both files are PyTorch checkpoints of about 280 MB, saved with torch.save. Each one is a dictionary rather than a bare state dict, with these keys:

  model  the weights
  arch   the timm backbone name, coatnet_rmlp_2_rw_384.sw_in12k_ft_in1k
  res    the input size the model expects, 384
  lab    the twelve finding names, in the order the model outputs them
  epoch  which training epoch the weights come from

raptor_ft_coatnet_v4_full.pt is the single best training epoch, and is the checkpoint that produced the 0.924 score.

raptor_ft_coatnet_v4_full_swa.pt is the same training run with the weights of its three best epochs averaged into one. Averaging weights this way costs nothing at inference and often gives a small gain, but on this particular run it did not, which is why the plain checkpoint is the one that was used.

THE MODEL

A CoAtNet backbone at 384 pixels with an attention pooling head on top.

The model never sees a whole study at once. It sees a sequence of windows, where each window is three neighbouring slices stacked into the three colour channels, and it pools those windows into one score per finding. Reading three slices at a time gives it some sense of what lies above and below the middle slice, which is most of the benefit of a 3D network at the cost of a 2D one.

The pooling layer has separate attention weights for each of the twelve findings. A cruciate tear may be visible on two slices while osteoarthritis is spread across many, so each finding is allowed to decide for itself which slices matter instead of sharing one pooled view.

HOW IT WAS TRAINED, AND WHY THAT IS THE INTERESTING PART

The competition gives you 4,407 studies but structured labels for only 58 of them. Every other study comes with a free-text radiology report and nothing else. So the first problem is not the model, it is that there is almost nothing to train against.

The labels used here were produced by reading those reports with a language model and turning each one into twelve probabilities rather than twelve yes or no answers. A report saying a tear is suspected becomes a number near 0.8, not a 1. Training on soft targets like these is more forgiving than forcing every uncertain report into a hard label.

That gives 4,349 studies to train on. The 58 studies that came with real labels were kept back and never trained on, and are used to check the model honestly. It reaches 0.9167 macro-AUC on them.

No external data was used.

HOW TO USE THEM

The weights expect their input to be built in a particular way, so loading them on their own is not enough. The companion notebook does the whole job end to end and is the easiest place to start:

https://www.kaggle.com/code/dreaddevelopment/knee-mri-twelve-findings-from-a-single-model

In short, each study is turned into a fixed stack of 64 images by filling five slots: 18 slices from a sagittal series, 14 from a second sagittal series, 12 from a coronal series, 8 from a second coronal series and 12 from an axial series. Slices are taken evenly across 6 to 94 percent of each series, cropped to a 140 mm box using the pixel spacing in the DICOM header so that a knee fills the same fraction of the frame whatever the scanner did, and resized to 336 pixels. The model then runs over three-slice windows taken from that stack, at 384 pixels, with ImageNet normalisation.

Loading a checkpoint looks like this:

  import torch, timm
  ck = torch.load("raptor_ft_coatnet_v4_full.pt", map_location="cpu", weights_only=False)
  backbone = timm.create_model(ck["arch"], pretrained=False, num_classes=0)
  # attach the attention head defined in the notebook, then:
  # model.load_state_dict(ck["model"], strict=True)
